I think the next big frontier for all of this work is figuring out how to reach and educate the majority of the population who do not already interact with the scientific community - and many people who already do. I work with researchers at FWRI who are not familiar with the reason behind fertilizer bans, who think that perfectly clear water and white sterile sand are the healthiest ecosystems for marine wildlife, and that seawalls are the safest way to prevent erosion and flooding. The level of local marine/bay education regarding the topics in this survey is even lower amongst my neighbors and non-science friends. 

I'm not sure how to best reach the general public, but I can attest that many/most are eager to learn how to help. I'm in a crochet club, and about 2/3rds of the older women in the group said that they hand-wash their dishes to conserve water "for the manatees and fish." When I showed them resources about dishwashers actually using less water than handwashing, they were all appalled at their misconception and eager to start using their dishwashers. We had a similar conversation regarding drip-line irrigation vs. hose watering by hand, fertilizer use in summer, and how to identify sustainable seafood options. Most people that I speak to are eager to learn and help, but they don't know where to find the information - or are bombarded by mis-information via viral click-bait/AI posts on facebook. I did see y'alls fertilizer info on the side of a bus last week (I think that was from TBEP) and thought it was great! 

I will suggest that figuring out how to get your information/education to the top of google/bing results from local searches would be helpful. I've recently discovered that most people I am around don't include "in Florida" or "in St. Pete FL" in their google searches, so they get irrelevant information regarding native plants or best water practices from other parts of the country/world. And even when I do a search for "are seawalls good Tampa", I get mixed answers and TBEP is nowhere in the top results. However, I know the bigger question is how do we get people to even think about whether or not seawalls are good - and other than an often-repeated local news story, I'm not sure how to do that.
